title: How to Solve CBSE Class 12 Maths Case Study Questions (With Examples)
meta_title: Solve CBSE Class 12 Maths Case Study Questions
meta_desc: A clear 5-step method to solve CBSE Class 12 Maths case study questions, with two worked examples, the chapters they come from, and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Case study questions scare students less because of the maths and more because of the paragraph in front of it. Here is the exact way I teach students to break them open, with two full worked examples and a quick self-test.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Open any recent CBSE Class 12 Maths paper and you will find a question that starts with a story — a factory owner deciding how many tables and chairs to build, a doctor reading a diagnostic test, a farmer fencing a rectangular plot. Then come three or four sub-questions worth four marks in total. Most students who lose those marks do not lose them because the maths is hard. They lose them because they read the paragraph once, panic, and start hunting for a formula before they have understood what is being asked.

Case study questions — sometimes called competency-based or source-based questions — now make up a real chunk of the Class 12 board paper. The good news: they are almost always built on chapters you have already studied hard for. The scenario is a costume; the maths underneath is ordinary. Here is how to see through the costume every time.

Which chapters CBSE case study questions come from

Case study questions in Class 12 Maths are not random. Over the last few years they have clustered around a handful of chapters that lend themselves to real-life setups. Knowing the usual suspects tells you which concept to reach for before you have even finished reading.

ChapterTypical case study scenarioWhat it tests
ProbabilityA medical test, two machines making defective parts, drawing cardsConditional probability, Bayes theorem, total probability
Application of DerivativesMaximising area or profit, minimising cost or materialMaxima and minima, second-derivative test
Linear Programming (LPP)A factory mixing two products under resource limitsFeasible region, corner-point method
Matrices & DeterminantsTicket sales, cost of items bought in different quantitiesMatrix operations, solving equations, area of a triangle
IntegralsArea under a curved arch, distance from a velocity functionDefinite integration, area between curves

If you have revised these five chapters properly, you are ready for roughly nine out of ten case studies. Probability and Application of Derivatives, in my experience, are the two that appear most often, so give them extra attention.

The 5-step method that works on every case study

The trick is to slow down at the start so you can speed up later. I teach the same five steps to every student, and the ones who follow them stop leaving marks on the table.

Step 1 — Read the scenario twice, pencil in hand

Read it once for the story, once for the numbers. On the second pass, underline every number and every condition. A phrase like ‘the sum of the two dimensions is 20’ is a constraint you will need, not decoration.

Step 2 — Extract the data as symbols

Turn the words into variables before you touch a formula. Let the length be x, let the probability of the first machine be P(A), and so on. Half the marks are lost by students who keep juggling words in their head instead of writing x and y on paper.

Step 3 — Identify the concept

Ask one question: which chapter is this? ‘Find the maximum’ screams Application of Derivatives. ‘Given that the part is defective, find the probability it came from…’ is Bayes theorem, every single time. Naming the concept tells you which formula to set up.

Step 4 — Solve the sub-parts in order

Case studies are built as a staircase. Part (i) usually feeds part (ii). Do them in sequence and reuse your earlier answer instead of starting fresh each time. Show the substitution clearly — step marks are real.

Step 5 — Sanity-check the answer

A probability above 1, a negative length, a maximum profit smaller than the minimum — these are all signals you slipped. Spend the last ten seconds asking whether the number could be true in the real world the question described.

Worked example 1: an Application of Derivatives case study

A farmer has 40 metres of fencing to enclose a rectangular vegetable plot along a straight wall, so only three sides need fencing. He wants the largest possible area.

Let the two sides perpendicular to the wall be x each and the side parallel to the wall be y. Fencing used: 2x + y = 40, so y = 40 − 2x. Area A = x y = x(40 − 2x) = 40x − 2x².

Differentiate: A′ = 40 − 4x. Set A′ = 0, so x = 10. Check the second derivative: A″ = −4, which is negative, confirming a maximum. Then y = 40 − 20 = 20, and the maximum area is 10 × 20 = 200 square metres. Notice how naming the concept in Step 3 handed us the whole plan.

Worked example 2: a Probability (Bayes) case study

In a factory, Machine A makes 60% of the bolts and Machine B makes 40%. Of A’s bolts, 2% are defective; of B’s, 5% are defective. A bolt picked at random is found defective. What is the probability it came from Machine B?

Extract the data: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.4, P(defective | A) = 0.02, P(defective | B) = 0.05. By Bayes theorem, P(B | defective) = [P(B)⋅P(def | B)] ÷ [P(A)⋅P(def | A) + P(B)⋅P(def | B)]. The numerator is 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.02. The denominator is (0.6 × 0.02) + (0.4 × 0.05) = 0.012 + 0.02 = 0.032. So the answer is 0.02 ÷ 0.032 = 0.625. A sanity check: B is the sloppier machine, so it should account for more than half the defectives — and 0.625 agrees.

Common mistakes that cost easy marks

  • Skipping the second-derivative (or corner-point) test, so the examiner cannot see you confirmed it was a maximum.
  • Mixing up P(A | B) with P(B | A) — read which event is ‘given’ very carefully.
  • Writing only the final answer for each sub-part and losing the step marks in between.
  • Forgetting units in mensuration-style questions — square metres, rupees, litres.
  • Not defining variables, then getting lost halfway through a long LPP setup.

Practise with real case study questions

Reading a method is one thing; the marks come from doing twenty of these until the pattern feels obvious. Try the free 8-question quiz below — it mixes probability, derivatives, LPP and matrices so you have to identify the concept yourself, just like the board paper. When you want a full graded set with worked solutions, the Class 12 case-studies bundle linked at the end covers every chapter with exam-style scenarios and step-by-step answer keys.

quiz.title: Class 12 Maths Case Study Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight board-style case study questions across probability, derivatives, LPP and matrices. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: CBSE Class 12 Maths case study / competency questions

questions.q: A case study begins ‘A rectangular plot with perimeter 40 m is to have maximum area.’ Which chapter does this test?
questions.explanation: ‘Maximum area’ means maxima and minima, which is Application of Derivatives. You differentiate the area, set it to zero, and confirm with the second-derivative test.

questions.q: A rectangle has perimeter 40 m. Using x and y for its sides, its maximum area occurs when it is a square of side 10 m. What is that area?
questions.explanation: With 2x + 2y = 40, area is maximised at x = y = 10, giving 10 × 10 = 100 square metres.

questions.q: ‘Given that the item is defective, find the probability it came from Machine A.’ Which result should you use?
questions.explanation: The phrase ‘given that…find the probability it came from…’ is the signature of Bayes theorem (reverse conditional probability).

questions.q: Machine A makes 70% of parts (1% defective) and Machine B makes 30% (4% defective). What is P(defective)?
In a Linear Programming case study, the maximum or minimum of the objective function is always found at…
options: The centre of the feasible region
A corner (vertex) of the feasible region
questions.explanation: The corner-point method: the optimum of a linear objective over a bounded feasible region occurs at one of its vertices.

questions.q: A shop sells x pens at ₹10 and y notebooks at ₹30, total sales ₹900. As a matrix equation this is one row. If y = 20, what is x?
A case study asks for the area under the curve y = x² from x = 0 to x = 3. Which tool solves it?
questions.explanation: Area under a curve between two limits is a definite integral: the integral of x² from 0 to 3 equals 27÷3 = 9 square units.

questions.q: You compute a conditional probability in a case study and get 1.25. What should you do?
options: Recheck — a probability can never exceed 1
questions.explanation: A probability must lie between 0 and 1, so 1.25 signals an arithmetic slip. The Step 5 sanity check catches exactly this kind of error.

faq.q: How many marks are case study questions worth in Class 12 Maths?
faq.a: In recent CBSE papers, case study (competency-based) questions typically appear in Section E and carry around 4 marks each, split across three or four sub-parts. Getting the sub-parts in order is the fastest way to bank those marks.

faq.q: Which chapters should I revise most for case study questions?
faq.a: Probability and Application of Derivatives appear most often, followed by Linear Programming, Matrices & Determinants, and Integrals. Master those five and you are ready for almost every case study.

faq.q: Are case study questions harder than normal questions?
faq.a: The maths is usually the same or easier — the difficulty is reading the paragraph correctly. Once you extract the numbers and name the concept, most case studies collapse into a routine calculation you have already practised.

faq.q: Do I need to show working, or is the final answer enough?
faq.a: Show every step. CBSE awards step marks for defining variables, setting up the formula, and substituting correctly. Students who write only the final answer routinely lose one or two marks per case study.

faq.q: Where can I get Class 12 case study questions with solutions to practise?
